title: 30 April 1943. A dead "Royal Marines officer" carried fake invasion plans.
description:
A dead "Royal Marines officer" carried fake invasion plans. The body was released from the submarine HMS Seraph so that it would be found. A fisherman found it.

Major William Martin never existed. British Military Intelligence invented him. His papers pointed to landings in Greece and Sardinia, with Sicily as a feint.

A letter between two generals named the wrong targets. It called Sicily and the Dodecanese "cover targets" for the real assaults.

Germany moved forces to the wrong places. Reinforcements went to Greece and Sardinia before and during the invasion of Sicily. Sicily received none.

The body was never an officer. In 1996 it was identified as Glyndwr Michael, a Welsh homeless man.

An amateur historian from London who found the evidence in the Public Record Office.

He was buried with full military honours as Major Martin. In 1998 a new inscription was added to the stone after the identification.

He fooled an army in death, and his real name stayed hidden for over fifty years.

Established the 30 April 1943 release from HMS Seraph; the persona Captain (Acting Major) William Martin of the Royal Marines; correspondence between two British generals suggesting invasion of Greece and Sardinia with Sicily a feint; the letter naming Sicily and the Dodecanese as "cover targets"; "German reinforcements were shifted to Greece and Sardinia before and during the invasion of Sicily; Sicily received none"; and that in 1996 Roger Morgan, an amateur historian from London, uncovered evidence in the Public Record Office.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyndwr_Michael: read in full. Established that the body was identified in 1996 as Glyndwr Michael, a Welsh homeless man; that Major William Martin was a persona invented by British Military Intelligence; that he was buried with full military honours in Huelva (grave No.1886); and that a new inscription was added in 1998 after the identification.
